children: , the hybrid-cloud, AI and quantum-computing company, finalized a $1 billion Commerce Department award for its Anderon subsidiary, adding federal backing to one of its biggest bets on domestic quantum-chip manufacturing. Shares drops 0.5% to $228.46.

IBM is putting another $1 billion of its own capital behind Anderon's 300-millimeter Albany foundry, taking the disclosed funding package to $2 billion before counting previous investment at the site. Early wafers are already moving through production, targeting superconducting qubits alongside the signaling and readout hardware needed to connect them. More quantum architectures are expected to follow, giving IBM a manufacturing platform that could reach well beyond its own processors if outside demand develops.

The valuation picture adds another angle. The chart puts IBM's $228.46 share price 5.91% below its GF Value estimate of $242.80, suggesting the market is still pricing in some execution risk despite the government-supported expansion. The financing structure clearly helps: Washington is covering half of the newly disclosed $2 billion commitment, reducing the capital IBM must shoulder itself. But the commercial proof still has to arrive. IBM has not disclosed outside customers, purchase commitments, expected utilization or revenue targets for the foundry, leaving the biggest question unchanged: whether Anderon becomes an industry manufacturing asset or remains primarily a strategic piece of IBM's own quantum roadmap.

title: IBM Drops as $2 Billion Builds a Quantum Manufacturing Platform
